A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work despite the changed title and organization. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, figures, and tables are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: Section 4 and Figure 1 report original numerical measurements of robust GD stability under poisoning, a tailored Byzantine attack, and a no-attack reference condition.

after.justification: Section 4 and Figure 1 report original numerical generalization-error results under optimal poisoning and a revised tailored Byzantine attack, with experimental details in Appendix E.2.

M1.justification: The robust GD/SGD updates and SMEA aggregation rule are retained. The tailored Byzantine procedure changes: v1 Algorithm 1 starts with a poisoning step and subsequently branches on the parameter sign; v2 Algorithm 2 immediately selects extremal updates using the pivot worker's initial gradient.

E1.justification: Both numerical studies use the same constructed one-dimensional linear-loss task with honest and corrupted workers. No evaluated dataset, domain, or task is added or removed; v1's removed nonconvex coverage was theoretical.

E2.justification: Figure 1 removes the numerical no-attack reference. Optimal poisoning and tailored Byzantine comparisons remain, with the latter using a substantively revised attack. CWTM was not an evaluated empirical baseline in either version.

E3.justification: Figure 1 switches from uniform stability to generalization error using the documented factor 1/[4(n-f)]. Both versions retain n=15, m=1, T=5, learning rate and Lipschitz constant equal to 1, and f ranging from 1 to 7.

E4.justification: V1 Appendix E.1 estimates empirical robustness coefficients and substitutes them into the Byzantine upper bound to examine tightness. V2 removes this diagnostic and instead compares numerical errors with its new Byzantine lower bound for f>=n/3.

E5.justification: Both numerical validations use deterministic GD and display point values without repeated-run statistics, error bars, or significance tests. V2 omits v1's caption explanation for not reporting variance, but the statistical reporting practice is unchanged. Appendix G contains theoretical probability bounds in both versions.

E6.justification: The poisoning curve is unchanged after accounting for the stated rescaling. The Byzantine curve changes beyond rescaling under the revised attack, while retaining the finding of greater error than poisoning. No-attack results and the empirical-coefficient bound series are removed; these revisions do not establish a same-protocol performance gain.

T1.justification: V2 adds a constructive Byzantine stability lower bound in Theorem 3.2 and Appendix C.3, plus the generalization-separation theorem 4.2. Lemma 4.1 generalizes the calculation already present in v1 Appendix E.2. Conversely, v1's nonconvex theorems, CWTM properties and counterexample, and trace-based robustness results are removed rather than relocated.

C1.justification: The abstract's Byzantine contribution changes from an O(sqrt(f/(n-2f))) upper bound to an Omega(sqrt(f/(n-2f))) lower bound. V2 centers its contributions on formal convex SMEA separation for f>=n/3 and withdraws v1's nonconvex contribution.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly identifies the unresolved order of the gap for f<n/3 and explains why poisoning regularity improves generalization bounds without improving already-tight optimization guarantees. New Appendix H substantially expands discussion of practical relevance, other optimizers, multiple local steps, locally poisonous models, and targeted attacks, distinguishing these extensions from established results.

D1.justification: V2 documents revised attack triggering logic and an explicit lower-bound attack construction, while removing empirical robustness-coefficient estimation instructions. Experimental parameters, worker identities, and epsilon=0.001 are retained. New Algorithm 1 contains a threshold inconsistency: its g1<=C condition does not distinguish the unperturbed value C from the smaller perturbed value described in the proof.

R1.justification: V2 adds Bousquet, Klochkov and Zhivotovskiy (2020) as the source for Appendix G's probability bounds, replacing Lugosi and Neu (2022). Several background and nonconvex-analysis references are removed, including Charles and Papailiopoulos (2018) and Le Bars et al. (2024). The principal positioning against robust optimization and decentralized stability work remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statement, and Sections 3–4 are extensively rewritten. SMEA's definition moves into the preliminaries, GD/SGD upper-bound proofs are consolidated, cryptographic implications move to the conclusion, and the appendices are reorganized around the two threat models.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main text and references with redesigned headers and appendix formatting. Figure 1 changes its axis, curves, legend, and regime markings; Table 1 and a Byzantine-construction diagram are added. V1's two CWTM illustrations are removed, and the attack pseudocode displays change.

improvement.justification: V1 relied on upper-bound comparisons and numerical evidence for Byzantine tightness. V2's constructive lower-bound argument and generalization-separation theorem substantially strengthen the central scientific justification, while explicit regime qualifications clarify what remains unresolved. Removing nonconvex/CWTM coverage narrows the paper, and Algorithm 1 retains a localized threshold inconsistency, but the central convex analysis is substantially better supported.
